deepDive: PNG to JPG is the classic trade in image conversion: moving from lossless to lossy. The browser first decodes the PNG into an RGBA pixel grid—that step is exact—then flattens the alpha channel onto a solid background (white by default), and finally slices the image into 8×8 blocks, applies a discrete cosine transform and quantizes away the high-frequency coefficients. Those coefficients are the only thing actually lost.

How much smaller the file gets depends on the content, not on the tool. Screenshots, flat UI and line art already compress extremely well in PNG, so a JPG version may only save 20–40% and will soften text edges. Photographs, gradients and noisy images barely compress at all in PNG, and often drop to a tenth of their size as JPG.

The test is simple: if the image relies on transparency, contains text you need to zoom into, or will be edited again, keep the PNG. If it is going into a chat, a web page or a slide deck, the size advantage of JPG is very real.

deepDive: WebP is the only mainstream format that beats PNG on both counts at once: lossless quality and full transparency. Its lossless mode (VP8L) preserves every pixel and the complete alpha channel, which makes PNG to WebP a genuinely free diet for web assets.

The savings come in two tiers. Lossless WebP is typically 20–30% smaller than PNG. If you accept lossy mode, photographic content drops another 60% or more while still carrying an alpha channel—a combination JPEG cannot offer at any setting.

The caveat is delivery. Files sent to clients, drops into older Office or WPS documents, and uploads to e-commerce or government portals that whitelist only jpg/png may all be rejected. Keeping a PNG copy alongside is far cheaper than fixing it later.

deepDive: To understand PNG to ICO, first understand that ICO is a container rather than an image. A single .ico file can hold 16×16, 32×32, 48×48 and 256×256 versions, and Windows or the browser picks whichever suits the context.

Composition matters too. The system applies a safe zone when cropping, so artwork that touches the edge can get clipped. A square source with 5–10% padding all round produces the most reliable result.

The cost is size. Photographic JPGs typically expand 3–10× as PNG, because DEFLATE has almost nothing to work with on high-frequency content. If the goal is archiving or sharing, skip this conversion.

The one technical detail worth watching is bit depth. JPG is 24-bit true color and maps cleanly to 24-bit BMP; if the target application only accepts 8-bit or 16-bit BMP, you get color quantization and visible banding across gradients.

deepDive: HEIC has been the iPhone's default capture format since iOS 11, using HEVC to pack a photo into roughly half the size of JPEG. The conversion is a decode followed by a re-encode: the HEVC frame is decompressed to pixels and then written by a JPEG encoder. Decoding HEIC in the browser requires an extra WebAssembly library, which this site bundles and loads on demand—so the first conversion takes a second or two longer.

Quality is not a concern. HEIC originals are usually cleaner than a JPEG of the same resolution, so a high-quality JPG looks essentially identical. The file simply gets bigger—the price of compatibility.

faqExtra.answer: Technically yes, but there is little point: HEIC's benefit is small files, and going from PNG to HEIC produces a similar-sized file with no quality gain.

faqExtra.question: Why is it slower than JPG conversion?
faqExtra.answer: HEIC requires loading a WebAssembly decoder, so the first conversion pays a one- or two-second initialization cost. Later conversions in the same session are much faster.

deepDive: SVG is a vector description and PNG is a pixel grid, so this conversion is rasterization: pick an output size, then draw the paths, fills and strokes at that size. Whatever size you choose is baked in—scaling it up afterwards blurs, exactly like a screenshot.

That makes the important parameter size and scale factor rather than "quality". For web use, export at 2× the display size so high-DPI screens stay crisp. For print, work back from 300 DPI: an A4 width of 210 mm is roughly 2480 pixels.

Fonts are the other common trap. If text in the SVG was not converted to outlines, a rendering environment lacking that font will substitute another and the layout will break. Outlining text in the source file is the cheapest insurance.

mechanics.label: Parse
mechanics.value: Read SVG path, fill and stroke instructions

mechanics.label: Set size
mechanics.value: Create a canvas at the target pixel dimensions

whenNot: Infinite scalability is required—keep the SVG
Large-format print output where final size is undecided
The SVG relies on heavy filters or blend modes that rasterize differently
svg-to-png.compat: PNG is universal. Once rasterized, an SVG that only a browser could display can go into Word, PowerPoint, WeChat, social platforms—anywhere at all.

faqExtra.question: Does converting to PNG reduce quality?
faqExtra.answer: It is sharp at the export size, but scaling that PNG up later will blur because the pixels are fixed. Export at the largest size you will ever need.

faqExtra.question: What size should I export?
faqExtra.answer: For web, twice the display size (2×). For print, calculate from 300 DPI—a 10 cm width corresponds to about 1181 pixels.

faqExtra.question: Is the transparent background kept?
faqExtra.answer: Yes. SVG has no background concept, so areas not covered by artwork become transparent pixels, which PNG preserves exactly.

faqExtra.question: Why did the text change position or font?
faqExtra.answer: Fonts referenced by the SVG fall back when unavailable in the rendering environment. Convert text to outlines in your design tool before exporting.

faqExtra.question: Can the PNG be used for print?
faqExtra.answer: Yes, provided you export enough pixels for print resolution—and note that the result stays RGB, so it still needs a CMYK conversion for prepress.

deepDive: SVG to JPG usually has one driver: the destination only accepts JPG—an e-commerce backend, a social upload endpoint, or an old document system. Otherwise JPG has no advantage here, since it cannot do transparency and it introduces compression noise along vector edges.

One decision comes before everything else: the background color. Empty areas in an SVG are transparent, and JPG must have a solid fill. White suits most document and web contexts; a brand color or dark tone needs care, since it can collide with the artwork.

There is a detail that is easy to overlook: vector art is made of high-contrast sharp edges, which is exactly where JPG compression performs worst. Colored speckles and blocky blur appear near strokes, so use a generous quality setting—or just use PNG.

mechanics.label: Background
mechanics.value: Fill transparent areas with a solid color

mechanics.label: Rasterize
mechanics.value: Draw at the target size with anti-aliasing

whenNot: Transparency is required—JPG cannot do it
The artwork is mostly thin lines and small text
The image will be reused on the web many times
svg-to-jpg.compat: JPG is the most widely accepted format anywhere. If the target system only takes JPG, this is the only route in.

faqExtra.question: What color do transparent areas become?
faqExtra.answer: JPG requires an opaque background, so transparent regions are filled with a solid color—white by default. Use SVG to PNG if you need transparency.

faqExtra.question: Why are there colored speckles along the edges?
faqExtra.answer: JPG quantizes away high-frequency detail, and vector edges are almost entirely high frequency. That produces mosquito noise and color fringing—a format characteristic, not a conversion error.

faqExtra.question: How do I choose the export size?
faqExtra.answer: Base it on the final display or print size; rasterized output cannot be enlarged losslessly. For web use 2×, for print 300 DPI.

faqExtra.question: Will text inside the graphic change?
faqExtra.answer: If the SVG's text was not outlined, rendering depends on system fonts and will fall back when one is missing. Outlining the text prevents this entirely.

faqExtra.question: Can it be converted back to SVG?
faqExtra.answer: No. Raster-to-vector requires tracing, which only approximates outlines and cannot recover the original paths or layer structure.

deepDive: TIFF is the standard for print and archival work, preserving CMYK, 16-bit depth and multi-page content losslessly—at the cost of enormous files and no browser support. Converting to JPG has a clear purpose: making the image openable in web pages, email, chat and ordinary software.

There is a limitation that must be stated plainly: mainstream browsers have no built-in TIFF decoder, and this site does not run server-side decoding. The browser-based conversion therefore cannot be completed; the page is explicitly marked unavailable and kept noindex so search users are not misled.

Where professional software is available, the right approach is to open the TIFF in Photoshop, XnView, ImageMagick or the system preview tool and export a JPG: convert print artwork to sRGB first, drop to 8 bits per channel, then export at quality 90 or above. That preserves detail while shrinking the file to a fraction of its size.
whenNot: Prepress delivery, where TIFF and CMYK must be kept
Multi-page or layered structure matters
Lossless archival precision is required
tiff-to-jpg.compat: JPG is universal—that is the point of converting. Do it locally in professional software rather than expecting it in a browser, since TIFF decoding is outside what browsers provide.

faqExtra.question: Why is this conversion unavailable here?
faqExtra.answer: Browsers ship no TIFF decoder and this site does not run server-side decoding. To avoid misleading visitors, the page states this clearly and is marked noindex.

faqExtra.question: How should I convert it then?
faqExtra.answer: Use Photoshop, Affinity Photo, XnView MP, ImageMagick (magick a.tif a.jpg), macOS Preview or the Windows Photos app—any local tool that can export JPG.

faqExtra.question: What should I watch out for?
faqExtra.answer: Prepress TIFFs are usually CMYK; convert to sRGB before JPEG export or colors will look noticeably dark. Also reduce 16-bit depth to 8-bit, or many applications will misread the file.

faqExtra.question: Is quality lost?
faqExtra.answer: There is one lossy pass, but above quality 90 the visual difference is minor. The real risks are color space conversion and bit-depth reduction, not JPEG encoding itself.

faqExtra.question: What about multi-page TIFFs?
faqExtra.answer: Converting to JPG typically exports only the current page or splits into separate files. If page structure matters, convert to PDF instead.

deepDive: TIFF to PNG differs from TIFF to JPG in intent: both endpoints are lossless, so the goal is to become viewable without losing anything. PNG keeps every pixel and the alpha channel, which suits scans and design assets that need a previewable copy.

The same browser limitation applies: mainstream browsers cannot decode TIFF and this site has no server-side decoding, so the page is marked unavailable and kept noindex. That is the honest approach rather than a button that does nothing.

Locally, the right sequence is to convert CMYK to sRGB, drop 16-bit to 8-bit, then save losslessly as PNG. The file is larger than JPG but preserves every pixel—appropriate when further editing or exact reproduction matters.

mechanics.value: CMYK or grayscale converted to sRGB

whenNot: File size is sensitive—PNG will be larger
Multi-page structure must survive (use PDF)

tiff-to-png.compat: PNG displays everywhere, but the conversion on this page is unavailable. Complete it locally with professional software, then use or upload the resulting PNG.

faqExtra.question: Why does the page say unsupported?
faqExtra.answer: Browsers cannot natively decode TIFF and this site does not run server-side TIFF decoding. The page states that clearly and sets noindex to avoid misleading clicks.

faqExtra.question: Is PNG or JPG better for a TIFF source?
faqExtra.answer: Use PNG if you need further editing or alpha; use JPG for previews, sharing or archiving where small files matter. Neither preserves CMYK or multi-page structure.

faqExtra.question: Will colors shift?
faqExtra.answer: CMYK to sRGB clips some of the gamut, particularly saturated cyans and oranges. That is inherent to the color space conversion; prepress work should keep the original TIFF.

faqExtra.question: Can multi-page TIFFs be converted?
faqExtra.answer: Not into a single PNG. Multi-page TIFFs are better converted to PDF, or split into individual images and processed separately.

faqExtra.question: Any recommended local tools?
faqExtra.answer: ImageMagick on the command line is fastest (magick in.tif out.png). For a GUI, XnView MP, IrfanView, Photoshop or macOS Preview all work.

deepDive: GIF is the oldest animated format on the web and by far the least efficient: a 256-colour ceiling produces banding and dither noise, and frame-by-frame storage makes files absurdly large. WebP compresses better, but an in-browser converter runs into a hard constraint — the Canvas API decodes only the first frame of a GIF.

So this tool does first-frame extraction plus modern encoding: the 256-colour palette of frame one is expanded to 24-bit true colour and recompressed with the VP8 encoder. The typical result is one fifth to one tenth the original size, with banding and dither noise gone. That is fully sufficient when you want the picture and not the motion; it is not sufficient for stickers or tutorial animations where the motion is the content.

To keep the animation you need frame-by-frame encoding: Google's own gif2webp is the standard route, and ffmpeg can do it too (use -loop to control looping). Those are desktop tools — they do not run in a browser and do not upload your files anywhere.

mechanics.label: Decode
mechanics.value: First frame only (Canvas cannot decode multiple frames)

whenNot: The animation must survive (this tool exports the first frame only — use gif2webp or ffmpeg)
The destination only accepts GIF (some chat tools, forums, older apps)
Pixel-exact reproduction is required even for the still image (use lossless WebP and verify)
gif-to-webp.compat: Static WebP has no compatibility problem: Chrome 17+, Edge 18+, Firefox 65+ and Safari 14+ all support it. The caveat applies to animated WebP — the Windows Photos app shows only the first frame, and some chat clients treat the file as a still image.

faqExtra.question: Does the animation survive?
faqExtra.answer: No. Browsers decode only the first frame of a GIF, so this tool exports a still WebP of that frame. For animation, encode frame by frame with gif2webp or ffmpeg.

faqExtra.question: How much smaller?
faqExtra.answer: The first frame is usually 60–90% smaller. GIF's 256-colour limit forces dithering, and dithering makes an image very hard to compress; at 24-bit true colour that overhead disappears.

faqExtra.question: Is transparency kept?
faqExtra.answer: Yes, and upgraded: GIF offers 1-bit transparency (fully transparent or fully opaque), while WebP supports 8-bit alpha, so soft edges look far more natural.

faqExtra.question: Can I send the WebP on WeChat or QQ?
faqExtra.answer: Not advisable. Chat apps re-encode images on send, so your format never survives anyway, and sending it as a file raises the odds the recipient cannot open it. Convert to JPG if you just need to send a picture.
